title: Chapter 149 – Trial of the Seed
html:
[Azure Cloud Sect – Lin Jian]

Twelve years is long enough to learn the exact sound of the Gate.

Jian knows it as a sailor knows weather. In the first year it was a hush, with the soft occasional knock of the Archivist testing the wall. By the third it had become a slow breath, in and out. By the sixth it had learned the rhythm of his own, so that when he inhaled over the Seed it inhaled with him, and when he let go the stone sighed. He no longer hears it as something outside. It is a second pulse, a bass note beneath his own, and some nights, sitting cross-legged on the flat stone with the lamp burning low, he forgets which of the two is keeping time for the other.

The twelve years have not been quiet, but they have been kind.

Wuping died in the second winter, at eighty-one, in his bed, with a bowl of millet on the table and Pei Wanli's hand in his. His last words were an apology to the cat. Gu Mingzhe followed him the next spring, rich and absurd and loved, and left the Treasury's entire private fund to the Sect's school for the restored. Pei An read his last name at the Dock when he was seventy-nine, the name of the eleventh burned soul on Ye's old list, and sat afterward on the stair with a cup of tea and said that he felt as light as a leaf. He is still alive. He sits on the ridge most days with Ning Ruiyan, the two of them squinting at the sky.

The clan stands at eleven hundred and four. Lin Zhao has three children. Bell has a clinic, and a husband from the Law benches, and a habit of correcting her elders. Yue, at seventy-one, looks fifty; she talks with her hands, and listens to the earth, and spends most evenings in the Dock on her stool with Pebble on her lap, humming along with a sound that no one else can hear. Feng is ninety and thin as a reed. He is not sleeping any better. He is, as far as anyone can tell, happy.

Ning's ring has grown. When Jian visits the observatory, in the spring of the eleventh year, the chart on the wall bears a new column in red ink, nine years of nights, each a little longer than the last. Last winter the eleven stars were dark for seven hours.

"It is coming," says Ning, in his gentle vast voice. "I cannot say what. But it is not stopping."

"When?"

"The solstice after next." The scar through his eyebrow wrinkles. "I took the liberty of calculating. The dark will cover the whole night, Keeper. From dusk to dawn."

Jian nods. He has done the same sum. The Seed will flower on the night of the five thousand one hundred and tenth feeding, which falls, by a coincidence he does not believe in, on the longest night of the year.

* * *

It is the night of the four thousand three hundred and eighty-first feeding. He counts them. It is one of the few things the Seed asks of him, and he has found, to his surprise, that he likes the counting, the small clean arithmetic of an ordinary night: two points of Cell, a breath, a gold thread running down into the hollow in his Seal, and the quiet hum of something growing.

Behind him, at the foot of the stair, a tall figure stands in the dark with a staff.

Tian Mo is thirty-two. He has stood there on most of the nights of those twelve years, in the same spot, with the same grave face. He is a tall, spare, silent man now, with Kuang's heavy shoulders and none of his talk, and the Sect pupils who train under him say that he has never been seen to sit. He nods when Jian looks round. He does not speak. It is a conversation they have had four thousand times.

"Tea?" says Qinghe, from the stool by the wall.

"Thank you."

She pours it. She is a hundred and three years old, and looks forty-five, and she has missed, by Jian's count, eleven suppers in twelve years. She sits on the stool she planted by the wall on the first night, in her blue smock, with a basket and a thermos, and watches him as she watches everything, with a sharp, tender, practical eye.

"The wall is quiet," she says.

"Yes."

"It is always quiet before." She hands him the cup. "Your father says to tell you the apples are early. He's awake, you know. He's been up three days."

"In midsummer?"

"He says it's the heat." She sniffs. "I say he cannot bear to miss the fuss."

He smiles. He sips. The tea is hot and bitter and tastes faintly of ginger, and the Seed, resting in the hollow of his Seal, pulses once, warm and golden, like a heart.

Then the panel opens.

* * *

* * *

```
ARK-3 :: CORE SEED :: NIGHT 4,381 / 5,110
SEED STAGE: Bud
SEAL: 72%
GATE LINK: Established (tuned)
TRIAL CONDITION: Seal >= 60% during Bud.
COLE DOOR: PAGE 2 :: UNLOCKED
PAGE 3 :: UNLOCKED (Seed-bound)
NOTE: A core cannot flower in a man who does not know what he carries.
REQUIRED: Read pages 2 and 3 before night 5,000.
```

He sets the cup down very carefully.

For twelve years the Cole door has been a closed thing at the end of a side passage, a gray slab under a curtain of roots. He has walked past it every night, on the way up to supper, and each time he has put out a hand and touched it, as one touches a sleeping animal, and each time it has been cold. He had told himself that it was patience. He had told himself that it was a matter of numbers. Seventy-two percent. It had been sixty for nine years, and sixty-four, and sixty-eight. He had waited for each page with the dull good manners of a man waiting for a verdict.

"Jian?" says Qinghe.

"The door is open."

She does not ask which. She stands up. She is quick, for a woman of a hundred and three; she has the lantern in her hand before he has finished rising. And behind her, from the foot of the stair, comes the soft deliberate tread of Tian Mo's boots, advancing, unasked, into the lamplight.

"No," says Jian gently. "Not tonight. This one I walk alone."

"It is not safe."

"It is a room full of paper."

"It is Cole's," says Qinghe. "I don't care what's in it." Her lips are pressed white. "Go on. We'll be here."

He goes.

* * *

The side passage is as he remembers: low, damp, smelling of old roots. At the end of it the gray door stands open a hand's breadth, and a thin light, the color of old paper, spills out across the floor.

He pushes it.

It is a small room. He had forgotten how small. A table, a chair, a shelf of loose papers held down with stones. A lamp, with a chimney of thick glass, burning with a steady yellow flame that needs no fuel. The air is dry and cool and faintly sweet, like a library at dusk. On the table, squared with great care, lie three sheets of yellowed paper, one on top of another, each covered in a fine untidy hand.

He sits in the chair. He picks up the second sheet.

PAGE 2, it says, at the top, underlined twice. THE GATE. (I am sorry for the handwriting. I wrote this on a bad night.)

If you've come this far you've already worked out most of it, because you're me and I'm not stupid. So I'll skip the preamble. Here is what the Gate is. It is a copying surface. That's not poetry. I mean it literally, like a photocopier, if you remember what a photocopier is, and if you don't I'll explain later because it is genuinely funny. A very long time ago, in the place we were both born, I built a machine that could read a man all the way down, memory and habit and the little twist of reflex that makes a person the person he is, and put the whole record on a surface. A copy. Complete. I did it because I was dying and I was frightened and I had a daughter who was eleven.

Jian stops. He reads the word again. Daughter.

He has read the Cole logs of four Docks. He has read the tapes in the Orchard. In none of them had Ethan Cole ever mentioned a child.

Don't get excited. She's fine. She's older than I'll ever be. I'm explaining so you'll understand why I did what I did. I didn't want to leave her without a father, so I made a copy of him, a good one, and put it to sleep. That's the stored copy. He's in the first world, in the machine, on the surface, and he's asleep and he's as good as new and he is, in every sense I can defend, me.

Then I did the stupid part.

I thought: what if the copy could wake up somewhere else? What if the surface could be a door? I thought of it as a gift. A second chance for a version of me, somewhere new. I built the Gate to send a copy out and carry the world back. I didn't know that to send anything through, the Gate would have to be fed. I didn't know about the names. I didn't know what it would do to people. I only knew it worked.

It worked eight times.

* * *

He turns the page, and his hands are not quite steady.

Eight working copies. I call them Operators because I'm a coward and it sounds technical. Each one is a version of me, copied off the stored record, and placed in a newborn child in the new world, at the moment of the child's birth. The child must be expected. The child must be loved. I am sorry, I am so very sorry, but the placing cannot work otherwise. A copy of a man cannot live in an empty house; it needs a living mind to attach to. So the child stays. The child is a real child. The child is a person with his own name.

He doesn't go away, as far as I can tell. I used to think he did.

The Gate has a restore. If the Operator dies near a Dock, or near the Gate, the system flags it. It assumes failure. It restores the stored copy over the working one, and sends it back. It's a fail-safe, and I'm not proud of it. But it means that if the Operator dies, the working copy is gone, and the child...

The sentence is crossed out. Underneath it, in pencil, in a much steadier hand:

I don't know what happens to the child. I have never known. I'm sorry.

He reads it three times. He is aware of a cold, dry, spreading stillness, as of a man standing at the edge of a frozen lake and listening to the ice.

A note on photocopiers, since I promised: they were machines that made a second sheet of paper look exactly like the first by shining a very bright light across it. That's all. Everyone had one. Nobody was impressed. It is a great irony of my life that the greatest thing I ever built is, in its essentials, a photocopier that is very much too bright.

Now. The Seed.

I want you to understand that the Seed was never meant to make you strong. I know, in the world you're in, a core is a thing you grow for power, for years, for the sky. That's fine. Let them. But the version I wrote into your Seal is something else. It's a room. A small round room, inside you, with a door in it, where the two of you can sit down together and talk. That's all I could think of. I thought: if I can't give them a world, I can give them a table.

The message, the page goes on. If you've gathered all three fragments and sat the Seed, the Gate can run both ways, once. You get one message to the stored copy. He gets one back. I built that in at the end, in case I ever had to say sorry in person. What you say is your decision. But please, and I mean this, understand this one thing before you do.

It is not your decision.

It is the child's.

He's the one who lives in the house. You're the guest. If you speak for him, you're a thief. If you speak for yourself, you're a ghost. If you want to say anything to me at all, you must ask him first. And if he doesn't want to answer...

Then don't open the door.

P.S. There is a third page. I'd read it sitting down.

* * *

He does not go straight back for the third page.

He walks out of the little room, along the passage, past the curtain of roots, into the great dim round Dock, with the second page folded small in his fist. The Gate wall stands in the lamp-light like a closed eye. Qinghe is on her stool. She looks up when he comes out, and what she sees in his face makes her put down her cup.

"Sit," she says.

He sits. His legs have decided for him.

"There is a child," he says. His voice is a croak. "In me. A real one. He is the one you named. I am, I think, a guest. I have been wearing his name and his house for eighty-four years, and I never asked." He swallows. "Mother, I am so sorry. I should have known. I should have told you the day I woke."

Qinghe says nothing. She takes his hand in both of hers. They are small and warm and as strong as they ever were.

"I knew," she says.

He stares at her.

"Not in words. I am not a clever woman." Her thumbs move on his knuckles. "But you were never quite right, as a baby. You laughed at the wrong times. You looked at the lamp as if it were an insult. And then, sometimes, you did a thing that was entirely a child's: you'd hold your arms up to be lifted, or you'd put a stone in your mouth. Two of you. I could see the seam." She smiles, a bit crooked. "I thought, well, this is my son. He is a very odd one, and I do not mind."

"You never said."

"What would I have said? I know you are two people? To a child of three?" She shakes her head. "I loved you both. The one who came in late, and the one who was there before. I never felt I had to choose. I was just very careful to say your name to the one who was listening."

His throat tightens. "He was listening."

"I know that too." She leans forward and, without warning, kisses his white head, hard, on the crown. "He was listening when you broke the bowl. He was listening when you were afraid. All those times I sat by your bed, in the fever. I used to think I was talking to you, and then sometimes I thought I was talking to somebody else, and I did not know which of you I was comforting. It did not matter." Her voice shakes. "It never mattered. Go and read your page."

He nods. He cannot speak.

* * *

Yue is waiting on her stool by the south wall, with Pebble in her lap, and one look at his face is enough.

She signs, quickly, with both hands, the flat clear language Bell invented, and Pebble's small dry voice carries it across the gap into Jian's mind like a message passed hand to hand. You've read it.

"Page two."

And?

"The voice you heard." He sits down heavily on the floor beside her, with his back against her stool. "On the sixtieth night, through the Gate. Is the child all right? I think that was Ethan. The stored one. Asleep in the first world, talking in his sleep. He has been asking after the boy for twelve years, and I was never listening."

Yue's hands go still. Then they move, slowly, with the particular deliberate economy of someone choosing words. I thought it was asking about you.

"So did I."

It wasn't.

"No." He laughs, a small helpless sound. "He was asking about the other one. The one who lives in the house."

Yue looks at him for a long time. Her gray eyes are wide and clear and a little wet, and the hum of the world moves in them. She puts one hand on his white head, gently, as she did the night she took the jar.

Then you should ask him, she signs. Whoever he is.

"I'm afraid."

I know. A pause. So is he. I can hear it.

His heart drops. "You can hear him?"

A little. He's quiet. He sounds, Brother... Her mouth works. Pebble's voice, relaying, is very soft. He sounds like a boy holding his breath behind a door.

* * *

He goes back in alone, and shuts the door behind him.

He sits in the little room for what might be an hour, with the pale sheet in his hands and the lamp's steady flame standing straight in its chimney. The room is silent. Somewhere beyond the door, down the passage, a lantern moves, and a stool scrapes, and the Gate sighs in its sleep. He does not move.

The child stays.

He has known it. He has known it for twelve years, since the night at Peak, in the snow, when the panel said SHARED. He has known it as one knows the weather before the rain. But there is a great difference between knowing and reading, and the difference is the one Ethan Cole put in ink: a person with his own name.

Lin Jian.

It is the name Qinghe gave him. He has never doubted it. He has answered to it for eighty-four years, in a hundred thousand rooms, in the mouths of everyone he has loved. But he sits now, with the paper in his hand, and for the first time in his life he asks himself whose name it is.

He does not remember the first world. He has fragments: a lab, a cold coffee, a word like workstation. He remembers no daughter. He remembers no wife, no friend, no street. If there was a man who built this Gate, the man left no mark on Jian but a certain habit of mind and a taste for lists. He has never had another name. Nobody ever called him Ethan.

Lin Jian, he thinks. Lin Jian is the boy.

He puts the second page face down on the table, very gently, like a man laying a sleeping child in a cot. Then he lifts the third.

* * *

PAGE 3, it says. THE FORGETTING.

I'm going to tell you why you don't remember. I know you've wondered. You wake up in a child's body and you can't recall your own life, and you tell yourself it's the shock, or the transfer, or that the Gate was never exact. All of that's true, and none of it's the reason.

I took your memory on purpose.

I did it before the placing, when I made the copy. I wrote a seal across the record, a kind of lock, so that when you woke you'd have the habits and the skills, the shape of me, but not the story. I did it for the child's sake. A child can't grow up with a stranger's whole life sitting on top of his own. It would crush him. So I made it so you came as a guest. You'd have the mind. You'd have the judgment. You'd have, I hoped, enough of me to be useful. But you wouldn't have the pain.

And I made one other decision. This is the one I am least proud of.

I made the lock open when the child was ready.

His breath stops.

Not you. Him. The seal is keyed to the child's own signature. It opens when he consents. I thought: if he never wants me, I'll stay a guest all my life. I'll be a voice in his head and a pair of hands and nothing more. If he does, if some day he looks at me and says, "yes, you can stay," then the seal opens and I can tell him the rest. That's the arrangement. That's the whole of it. I got the idea from a bad novel.

So here is the truth, and I want you to sit with it.

You've never been in charge. You've been invited. And the boy who invited you has been awake, as far as the logs can tell, since the winter you were thirty.

* * *

The lamp does not flicker. The room is entirely still.

Jian reads the last paragraph twice, and then a third time, with the tips of his fingers pressed against the paper, as though he could feel through it.

He's awake, it says. He has been awake, listening, for fifty-four years. He hears everything you say. He sees through your eyes. He chose not to speak. I don't know why; I never do. Maybe he's shy. Maybe he's frightened of me. Maybe he's waiting for you to ask. But I'll tell you the one thing I do know, from watching seven of you.

The one who asks is the one who gets an answer.

Be kind to him. He's lived in a house with a stranger for his entire life, and he never complained once.

E.C.

He puts down the paper. He puts down his hands. He sits for a long time, perfectly still, with the dry cool air of the little room on his face, and he realizes with a distant, wondering horror that he is trying to remember the last time he spoke to himself aloud.

I have spoken a great deal, he thinks. I have said a hundred thousand words in this life, to everyone I have ever met.

I have never once said hello.

On the shelf the pile of loose papers shifts, with a soft dry rustle, and a single yellowed sheet slides to the floor. He picks it up. It is blank. And then, as he watches, the ink begins to come, drawn up from the grain of the paper in a thin gray line, as though some invisible hand were writing, very slowly, with great care, from the other side.

h e l l o

His heart stops.

It is not Ethan's hand. It is rounder, younger, more careful, the handwriting of a child who has been taught his letters by a mother with a ladle in her fist. It trembles. The strokes are uneven. Underneath, after a long pause, the pen begins again.

i didn't know how to start

i'm sorry it took so long

i'm lin jian

i think i was shy. also you were always so busy

please don't be afraid

The page goes still. The lamp burns on. And in the little room at the end of the passage, a white-haired man of eighty-four sits with a sheet of paper in his hands, and the tears run down his face, and for the first time in his life he says it aloud, in the voice of a stranger greeting someone he has loved for years.

"Hello."
